content: The Tai Chi Classics are a collection of manuscripts and commentaries that serve as authoritative guides for the proper study and practice of Tai Chi Chuan. These texts, which differ between schools, are traditionally written in classical Chinese and are utilized by modern schools tracing their lineage to the Chen family or through the Yang family. Despite claims of ancient origins by legendary authors, modern scholarship has not been able to date any of these texts earlier than the late 19th century. Among the writings considered as Tai Chi Classics are the following: 1. The Tai Chi Chuan Classic (T'ai Chi Ch'uan Ching, 太極拳經): This text is attributed to the legendary founder of Tai Chi Chuan, Zhang Sanfeng (張三豐), who is claimed to have lived during the 12th to 14th centuries. 2. The Salt Shop Manual (鹽店譜): This contains the Tai Chi Chuan Treatise (T'ai Chi Ch'uan Lun, 太極拳論), attributed to the legendary Wang Zongyue (王宗岳). The text was reportedly discovered in the back room of a Beijing salt shop by Wu Yuxiang's brother, Wu Chengqing (武澄清). 3. Miscellaneous Texts: These include the Song of Thirteen Postures, Mental Elucidation of the Practice of Tai Chi Chuan, and the Song of Sparring, which were passed down in the Yang and Wu families. 4. Texts by Wu Yuxiang (武禹襄, 1812–1880): Wu Yuxiang, a central figure in the Wu/Hao style of Tai Chi Chuan, and his relatives contributed significant writings to the tradition. 5. The Forty Chapters: These writings, preserved within the Yang and Wu families, are considered an important part of the Tai Chi literary tradition. 6. Tai Chi Chuan Illustrated (太極拳圖說): Published in 1919 by Chen Xin (陳鑫, 1849–1929), a prominent Chen family scholar, this work is a key text in the Chen family tradition. 7. The Study of Tai Chi Chuan (太極拳學): First published in 1924 by Sun Lutang (孫祿堂, 1861–1932), the founder of the fifth and final classical style of Tai Chi Chuan, this book is a significant contribution to the field. 8. Yang Chengfu's (楊澄甫, 1883–1936) Complete Principles and Applications of Tai Chi Chuan: Published in 1934, this work is regarded as authoritative in schools influenced by Yang Chengfu's many students and descendants. The book includes the famous Ten Essential Points of Taijiquan Theory, authored by Chengfu. 9. Wu Kung-tsao's (吳公藻, 1902–1983) Commentary on the Forty Chapters: Wu Kung-tsao provided original texts and commentary on the Forty Chapters in his book Wu Family Tai Chi Chuan (吳家太極拳), first published in Changsha in 1935. Wu's grandfather, Wu Quanyuo (吳全佑, 1834–1902), inherited the Forty Chapters from Yang Banhou (楊班侯, 1837–1890). When the book was republished in Hong Kong in 1980, the famous wuxia author Jin Yong contributed a postscript, discussing influences on Chinese martial arts from as far back as Laozi and Zhuangzi. Additionally, modern works such as Benjamin Lo's Tai Chi Chuan for Health and Self-Defense: Philosophy and Practice (1977), The Essence of T'ai Chi Ch'uan: The Literary Tradition (1979), and Douglas Wile's Lost T'ai-chi Classics from the Late Ch'ing Dynasty (1996) have further explored and preserved the Tai Chi literary tradition.
